jazz.explanation: "Jazz" means "jazz music". To say you like it, use it without an article: "Jeg kan godt lide jazz" (I like jazz).

jeg.explanation: "Jeg" means "I". To say who does something, use "jeg": "Jeg ser ham" (I see him). To say who it happens to, use "mig" (me): "Han ser mig" (He sees me).

jeg beklager.explanation: "Jeg beklager" means "sorry". It is the formal way to apologize, as in "Jeg beklager forsinkelsen" (I am sorry for the delay). For a quick sorry, like bumping into someone, say "undskyld" (sorry): "Undskyld, jeg ramte dig" (Sorry, I bumped into you).

jeg er ked af det.explanation: "Jeg er ked af det" means "I'm sad". When you regret something you did, it also means "I'm sorry": "Jeg er ked af det, jeg glemte din fødselsdag" (I'm sorry, I forgot your birthday). For a quick apology, like bumping into someone, say "undskyld" (sorry): "Undskyld, jeg ramte dig" (Sorry, I bumped into you).

jeg er uenig.explanation: "Jeg er uenig" means "I disagree". To say who you disagree with, add "med" (with): "Jeg er uenig med dig" (I disagree with you). To name the topic, add "i" (in): "Vi er uenige i det" (We disagree about that).

jeg forstår ikke.explanation: "Jeg forstår ikke" means "I don't understand". It is built from "forstår" (understand) and "ikke" (not). To say "I don't understand it", put "det" (it) before "ikke": "Jeg forstår det ikke". To ask someone to say it again, add: "Kan du gentage det?" (Can you repeat that?).

jeg glæder mig.explanation: "Jeg glæder mig" means "I'm looking forward to it". It literally says "I gladden myself", with "mig" (myself). To name what you look forward to, add "til" (to): "Jeg glæder mig til ferien" (I'm looking forward to the vacation).

jeg har det godt.explanation: "Jeg har det godt" means "I'm doing well". It literally says "I have it good", with "det" (it) after "har". To answer "Hvordan har du det?" (How are you?), say: "Jeg har det godt" (I'm doing well).

jeg har det skidt.explanation: "Jeg har det skidt" means "I'm not doing well". It literally says "I have it badly", with "skidt" (badly). To say it more gently, say: "Jeg har det ikke så godt" (I'm not doing so well).

jeg hedder….explanation: "Jeg hedder…" means "my name is…" and you add your name after it. It literally says "I am called…", from "at hedde" (to be called). To answer, the other person can say "Dejligt at møde dig" (Nice to meet you).

jeg kommer fra….explanation: "Jeg kommer fra…" means "I'm from…" and you add a country or town after it. It literally says "I come from…". To answer "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where are you from?), say: "Jeg kommer fra Danmark" (I'm from Denmark).

jeg vil gerne have.explanation: "Jeg vil gerne have" means "I would like". To order or ask for something politely, name the item after "have": "Jeg vil gerne have en kaffe" (I would like a coffee). Without "gerne" (gladly), "Jeg vil have en kaffe" (I want a coffee) is blunt.

jern.explanation: "Jern" means "iron", as in the metal. To talk about the mineral in food, use the same word: "Spinat indeholder jern" (Spinach contains iron). "En jernbane" (a railway) is built from "jern" and "bane" (track).

jetlag.explanation: "Jetlag" means "jet lag". Danish writes it as one word, "jetlag", where English writes two words.

jord.explanation: "Jord" means "earth / soil". To talk about a piece of land, use it with "et stykke" (a piece): "et stykke jord" (a plot of land).

jubel.explanation: "Jubel" means "cheering". It is the noun for the verb "at juble" (to cheer).

jul.explanation: "Jul" means "Christmas". To say when something happens, use "til jul" (at Christmas): "Vi ses til jul" (See you at Christmas). To talk about the whole season, use "i julen" (during the Christmas season): "Jeg læser meget i julen" (I read a lot during the Christmas season).

juleaften.explanation: "Juleaften" means "Christmas Eve". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "aften" (evening). To say today is that evening, use it without an article: "Det er juleaften i dag" (It is Christmas Eve today).

julepynt.explanation: "Julepynt" means "Christmas decorations". It is built from "jul" (Christmas) and "pynt" (decoration). To say you put them up, use it without an article: "Vi hænger julepynt op" (We hang up Christmas decorations).

juice.explanation: "Juice" means "juice". To name the fruit, put it in front of "juice", as in "appelsinjuice" (orange juice) or "æblejuice" (apple juice).

related.en: fruit cordial (a sweet syrup mixed with water)

juli.explanation: "Juli" means "July". Unlike English, Danish spells month names like ordinary words, so you write "i juli" (in July), not "i Juli".

juni.explanation: "Juni" means "June". Unlike English, Danish spells month names like ordinary words, so you write "i juni" (in June), not "i Juni".

jura.explanation: "Jura" means "law", as the subject you study at university: "Hun læser jura på universitetet" (She studies law at the university). To talk about one rule made by the state, use "en lov" (a law): "Det er en ny lov" (It is a new law).

juridisk.explanation: "Juridisk" means "legal", in the sense of law and courts. To call something a legal matter, say: "Det er et juridisk problem, ikke et politisk" (It is a legal problem, not a political one). Do not mix it up with "lovlig" (allowed by law): "Det er lovligt at parkere her" (It is legal to park here).

jysk.explanation: "Jysk" means "Jutlandic", from or about "Jylland" (Jutland), the part of Denmark that is joined to the rest of Europe. To talk about the way people speak there, use it as the name of the dialect: "Jeg forstår ikke jysk" (I do not understand Jutlandic).

jævnligt.explanation: "Jævnligt" means "regularly". It comes from "jævn" (even). Its opposite is "sjældent" (rarely): "Jeg ser ham sjældent" (I rarely see him).

jødedom.explanation: "Jødedom" means "Judaism". It is built from "jøde" (Jew) and "-dom". The ending "-dom" is also in "barndom" (childhood) and "kristendom" (Christianity).

jødisk.explanation: "Jødisk" means "Jewish". It comes from "en jøde" (a Jew). To name the religion, use "jødedom" (Judaism): "Han studerer jødedom" (He studies Judaism).

jøsses.explanation: "Jøsses" means "gosh". It is a mild exclamation, so it is not rude. To react to surprising news: "Jeg har vundet i lotteriet!" "Jøsses!" (I won the lottery! Gosh!)

at kalde.explanation: "At kalde" means "to call", as in giving a name. To name someone or something, say: "Vi kalder hunden Max" (We call the dog Max). For phoning, use "at ringe" (to phone): "Jeg ringer til dig" (I will call you).

at kalde på.explanation: "At kalde på" means "to call for". To call out so that someone comes, add the person after "på" (on): "Han kalder på sin mor" (He calls for his mother). Without "på", "at kalde" means to name: "Vi kalder hunden Max" (We call the dog Max).

at kaste.explanation: "At kaste" means "to throw". To throw something to someone, add "til" (to): "Jeg kaster bolden til dig" (I throw the ball to you). With "op" (up), it means "to vomit": "Jeg skal kaste op" (I am going to be sick).

at kaste håndklædet i ringen.explanation: "At kaste håndklædet i ringen" means "to give up". Literally, it is "to throw the towel in the ring". For a plain way to say it, use "at give op" (to give up): "Jeg giver op" (I give up).

at kaste op.explanation: "At kaste op" means "to throw up". It is built from "kaste" (to throw) and "op" (up). Without "op", "kaste" means to throw an object: "Jeg kaster bolden" (I throw the ball).

at kategorisere.explanation: "At kategorisere" means "to categorize". It comes from "en kategori" (a category).

at kede sig.explanation: "At kede sig" means "to be bored". To say you are bored, use "mig" (myself): "Jeg keder mig" (I am bored). The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with the person: "Han keder sig" (He is bored), "Vi keder os" (We are bored).

at kende.explanation: "At kende" means "to know", as in being familiar with a person or a place: "Jeg kender Anna" (I know Anna). To know a fact, use "at vide" (to know): "Jeg ved, at hun bor her" (I know that she lives here).

at kidnappe.explanation: "At kidnappe" means "to kidnap". The person who does it is "en kidnapper" (a kidnapper): "Politiet leder efter kidnapperen" (The police are looking for the kidnapper).

at kigge.explanation: "At kigge" means "to look". To tell someone to look, say: "Kig her!" (Look here!). To say what you look at, add "på" (at): "Jeg kigger på billedet" (I am looking at the picture). To tell a shop assistant you do not need help, say: "Jeg kigger bare" (I'm just looking).

at kigge efter.explanation: "At kigge efter" means "to look for". To say what you are searching for, put it after "efter" (for): "Jeg kigger efter mine briller" (I am looking for my glasses). When you watch over someone, it means "to keep an eye on": "Kig efter børnene" (Keep an eye on the kids).

at kildre.explanation: "At kildre" means "to tickle". To say you tickle someone, name the person after it: "Han kildrede mig på foden" (He tickled me on the foot). To say a spot feels ticklish, use "det kildrer" (it tickles): "Det kildrer i næsen" (My nose tickles).

at klappe.explanation: "At klappe" means "to clap / pat". To show you liked a show, clap your hands: "Publikum klapper" (The audience claps). To stroke a pet gently, pat it: "Jeg klapper hunden" (I pat the dog).

at klare.explanation: "At klare" means "to manage / cope". To say you handle a task, say: "Han klarer opgaven" (He manages the task). To say you pass a test, say: "Jeg klarede prøven" (I passed the test).

at klare op.explanation: "At klare op" means "to clear up", for weather that gets better: "Det klarer op i aften" (It will clear up this evening). For tidying a room, use "at rydde op" (to tidy up) instead: "Jeg rydder op på værelset" (I tidy up the room).

at klare sig.explanation: "At klare sig" means "to get by / do well". To say someone is doing well in a place, say: "Hun klarer sig fint i Danmark" (She is doing fine in Denmark). To say you manage without something, add "uden" (without): "Jeg klarer mig uden bil" (I get by without a car).

at klassificere.explanation: "At klassificere" means "to classify". It comes from "en klasse" (a class).

at klatre.explanation: "At klatre" means "to climb", as in going up with hands and feet. To say children climb a tree, say: "Børnene klatrer i et træ" (The children climb a tree). To say prices go up, use the same verb: "Priserne klatrer" (Prices are climbing).

at klemme.explanation: "At klemme" means "to squeeze / pinch". To say your finger got caught in a door, say: "Jeg klemte fingeren i døren" (I pinched my finger in the door).

at klikke.explanation: "At klikke" means "to click". To name the item you click, add "på" (on) before the item: "Jeg klikker på linket" (I click on the link). To click twice quickly, use "at dobbeltklikke" (to double-click): "Dobbeltklik på ikonet" (Double-click the icon).

at klippe.explanation: "At klippe" means "to cut (with scissors)". To cut paper with scissors, say: "Jeg klipper papir" (I cut paper). To say a hairdresser cuts hair, use the same verb: "Hun klipper mit hår" (She cuts my hair).

at klynge sig.explanation: "At klynge sig" means "to cling". To say what you cling to, add "til" (to): "Han klynger sig til rækværket" (He clings to the railing). The same pattern works for feelings: "Hun klynger sig til håbet" (She clings to hope).

at klæde.explanation: "At klæde" means "to suit". To say a color or clothes look good on someone, put the person after the verb: "Blåt klæder hende" (Blue suits her). With "sig" (oneself) it means dressing yourself: "Jeg klæder mig på" (I get dressed).

at klæde sig af.explanation: "At klæde sig af" means "to get undressed". The small word after "klæde" changes with the person: "Jeg klæder mig af" (I get undressed), "Hun klæder sig af" (She gets undressed). The opposite is "at klæde sig på" (to get dressed): "Jeg klæder mig på" (I get dressed).

at klæde sig på.explanation: "At klæde sig på" means "to get dressed". The small word "sig" (oneself) changes with the person: "Du klæder dig på" (You get dressed), "Han klæder sig på" (He gets dressed). To put on one item, say "at tage en jakke på" (to put on a jacket): "Jeg tager jakken på" (I put on the jacket).

at klø.explanation: "At klø" means "to itch / scratch". To say something itches, say: "Det klør" (It itches). To scratch yourself, add "sig" (oneself): "Jeg klør mig i hovedet" (I scratch my head).

at klø sig.explanation: "At klø sig" means "to scratch oneself". It is built from "at klø" (to itch / scratch) and "sig" (oneself). To name the body part you scratch, add "på" (on) before it: "Jeg klør mig på ryggen" (I scratch my back).

at knappe.explanation: "At knappe" means "to button". To say what you button, name it after the verb: "Han knapper skjorten" (He buttons the shirt). To open the buttons again, add "op" (up): "Jeg knapper jakken op" (I unbutton the jacket).

at knibe.explanation: "At knibe" means "to pinch / squint". To say someone pinched you, say: "Hun kneb mig i armen" (She pinched my arm). To say someone squints, add "øjnene sammen" (the eyes together): "Han kniber øjnene sammen" (He squints). When money is short, say: "Det kniber med pengene" (Money is tight).

at knuse.explanation: "At knuse" means "to crush". To say something broke into pieces, like glass, say: "Han knuste glasset" (He smashed the glass). It also works for feelings: "Det knuste hendes hjerte" (It broke her heart).

at knytte.explanation: "At knytte" means "to tie / connect". To clench a fist, say: "Han knytter næven" (He clenches his fist). To form a friendship, say: "De knytter et venskab" (They form a friendship). For tying shoelaces, use "at binde" (to tie): "Jeg binder mine snørebånd" (I tie my shoelaces).

at knække.explanation: "At knække" means "to crack / break". To say you break a stick, say: "Jeg knækker en pind" (I break a stick). For a broken bone, use "at brække" (to break): "Jeg har brækket armen" (I have broken my arm).

at knæle.explanation: "At knæle" means "to kneel". It comes from "et knæ" (a knee). To say someone proposed on one knee, say: "Han knælede og friede" (He knelt and proposed).

at koge.explanation: "At koge" means "to boil". To say water is bubbling hot, say: "Vandet koger" (The water is boiling). To boil food in water, name the food: "Jeg koger æg" (I boil eggs). For making a meal, use "at lave mad" (to cook): "Jeg laver mad" (I am cooking).

at koge over.explanation: "At koge over" means "to boil over". To say milk runs out of the pot, say: "Mælken koger over" (The milk boils over). It also works for feelings: "Hun koger over af vrede" (She is boiling over with anger).

at kollidere.explanation: "At kollidere" means "to collide". To name what you hit, add "med" (with): "Bilen kolliderede med en cykel" (The car collided with a bicycle). When two plans clash, use the same verb: "Mødet kolliderer med min tandlægetid" (The meeting clashes with my dentist appointment).

at kombinere.explanation: "At kombinere" means "to combine". To say which things you put together, join them with "med" (with): "Du kan kombinere en rød trøje med sorte bukser" (You can combine a red sweater with black trousers).

at komme.explanation: "At komme" means "to come". To say you are on your way, say: "Jeg kommer nu" (I am coming now). To ask where someone is from, use it with "fra" (from): "Hvor kommer du fra?" (Where are you from?). To say what will happen next, use "kommer til at": "Det kommer til at regne" (It is going to rain).

at komme an på.explanation: "At komme an på" means "to depend on". To answer a yes-or-no question when it is not clear, say: "Kommer du?" "Det kommer an på" (Are you coming? It depends). To name what it depends on, add it after "på" (on): "Det kommer an på prisen" (It depends on the price).

at komme for sent.explanation: "At komme for sent" means "to be late". Literally, it is "to come too late". To say you were late, say: "Jeg kom for sent til skolen" (I was late for school). For a train or bus, use "forsinket" (delayed): "Toget er forsinket" (The train is delayed).

at komme forbi.explanation: "At komme forbi" means "to come by". To invite someone to drop in for a visit, say: "Kom forbi i aften" (Come by tonight). To say you cannot pass something in the way, use it for "get past": "Vi kan ikke komme forbi bilen" (We cannot get past the car).

at komme frem.explanation: "At komme frem" means "to arrive / come forward". To say when a trip ended, say: "Vi kom frem klokken seks" (We arrived at six o'clock). To say someone stepped forward, say: "Han kom frem fra mængden" (He came forward from the crowd).

at komme godt ud af det med.explanation: "At komme godt ud af det med" means "to get along with". To say you have a good relationship with someone, say: "Jeg kommer godt ud af det med min chef" (I get along well with my boss). Put "dårligt" (badly) in place of "godt" (well) to say the opposite: "Jeg kommer dårligt ud af det med min nabo" (I get along badly with my neighbor).

at komme hjem.explanation: "At komme hjem" means "to come home". To ask when someone gets home, say: "Hvornår kommer du hjem?" (When will you get home?). To say you are setting off for home, use "at tage hjem" (to go home): "Jeg tager hjem nu" (I am going home now).

at komme i gang.explanation: "At komme i gang" means "to get started". To name the task you start, add "med" (with) and the task: "Jeg kom i gang med opgaven" (I got started on the task).

at komme i tanke om.explanation: "At komme i tanke om" means "to remember / think of". To say a thing suddenly came back to you, say: "Jeg kom i tanke om nøglerne" (I remembered the keys). To say you simply keep something in memory, use "at huske" (to remember): "Jeg husker hans navn" (I remember his name).

at komme ind.explanation: "At komme ind" means "to come in". To invite someone into a room, say: "Kom ind!" (Come in!). To say you could not get into a place, say: "Vi kom ikke ind i klubben" (We could not get into the club).

at komme med.explanation: "At komme med" means "to come along / bring". To ask if someone joins you, say: "Kommer du med?" (Are you coming along?). To say someone brought something, say: "Hun kom med kage" (She brought cake).

at komme ned.explanation: "At komme ned" means "to come down". To tell someone to come down from a high place, say: "Kom ned derfra!" (Come down from there!).

at komme op.explanation: "At komme op" means "to come up / get up". To invite someone upstairs, say: "Kom op til os!" (Come up to us!). To push someone to try harder, say: "Kom op!" (Come on!). To get out of bed, use "at stå op" (to get up): "Jeg står op klokken syv" (I get up at seven).

at komme over.explanation: "At komme over" means "to get over". To say someone never recovered from something hard, say: "Han kom aldrig over det" (He never got over it). To invite someone to visit you, say: "Kom over til os!" (Come over to our place!).

at komme sig.explanation: "At komme sig" means "to recover". It is built from "at komme" (to come) and "sig" (oneself). To name what you recover from, add "efter" (after): "Jeg kommer mig efter sygdommen" (I am recovering from the illness).

at komme til skade.explanation: "At komme til skade" means "to get hurt". To say when someone got hurt, say: "Han kom til skade i går" (He got hurt yesterday). To name the body part, add "på" (on) before it: "Jeg kom til skade på benet" (I hurt my leg).

at komme tilbage.explanation: "At komme tilbage" means "to come back". To say you will return soon, say: "Jeg kommer snart tilbage" (I will be back soon). The word "tilbage" (back) is also in "at give tilbage" (to give back) and "at betale tilbage" (to pay back).

at komme ud.explanation: "At komme ud" means "to come out / get out". To tell someone to leave a room, say: "Kom ud!" (Come out!). To say where someone comes out of, add "af" (of): "Han kommer ud af skolen" (He comes out of the school).

at komme videre.explanation: "At komme videre" means "to move on". To say you want to leave something painful behind, say: "Jeg vil gerne komme videre efter bruddet" (I want to move on after the breakup). To say you continue a trip, say: "Vi kom videre til næste by" (We went on to the next town).

at kommentere.explanation: "At kommentere" means "to comment". To say what you comment on, put it right after the verb, with no word for "on": "Hun kommenterer videoen" (She is commenting on the video).

at kommunikere.explanation: "At kommunikere" means "to communicate". To say which language you use, add "på" (in): "Vi kommunikerer på dansk" (We communicate in Danish). To name the person you communicate with, add "med" (with): "Jeg kommunikerer med kunden" (I communicate with the customer).

at kompensere.explanation: "At kompensere" means "to compensate". To name what you make up for, add "for" (for) before it: "Jeg kompenserer for fejlen" (I compensate for the mistake).

at komplicere.explanation: "At komplicere" means "to complicate". To say something makes matters harder, add "tingene" (the things): "Det komplicerer tingene" (That complicates things).

at komponere.explanation: "At komponere" means "to compose". To say who writes the music and who plays it, say: "Hun komponerer, og han spiller" (She composes and he plays).

at koncentrere sig.explanation: "At koncentrere sig" means "to concentrate". To say you cannot focus, say: "Jeg kan ikke koncentrere mig" (I cannot concentrate). To name the task you focus on, add "om" (on) before the task: "Vi koncentrerer os om opgaven" (We are concentrating on the task).

at konfirmere.explanation: "At konfirmere" means "to confirm", in the church ceremony where a young person confirms their baptism. In Denmark, the confirmation is followed by a family party called "en konfirmationsfest". To say you have been confirmed, say: "Jeg er konfirmeret" (I am confirmed).

at konkludere.explanation: "At konkludere" means "to conclude". To state the conclusion, add "at" (that) and a full sentence: "Jeg konkluderer, at planen virker" (I conclude that the plan works).

at konkurrere.explanation: "At konkurrere" means "to compete". To say who you compete with, add "med" (with): "Jeg konkurrerer med min bror" (I compete with my brother). To name the prize, add "om" (for): "Vi konkurrerer om prisen" (We compete for the prize).
